Free Developer Tools Online: JSON Formatter, Regex Tester, Base64, URL Encoder, JWT Decoder, SQL and UUID

By the DoraPDF team · 5 min read · Updated 2026-11-14

Every developer has a bookmark folder of tiny single-purpose sites: one to pretty-print JSON, one to test a regex, one to peek inside a token. DoraPDF keeps eight of these in one place, all free, all running in your browser, so pasted data stays on your machine. This is a practical tour of each free online developer tool: what it does, when to reach for it, and the gotchas worth knowing.

1. JSON Validator and Formatter

Use it when an API response is one unreadable line, or a config file refuses to load.

Paste your JSON into the JSON Validator. It checks the syntax as you type. Valid JSON shows a green "Valid JSON" status and a formatted copy in the output box. Choose 2 spaces or 4 spaces for indentation, or Minify to squash it back into one compact line for sending.

When the JSON is broken, the error message is shown, and in browsers that report a position, the tool converts it into a line and column so you can jump straight to the problem.

Usual suspects: a trailing comma after the last item, single quotes instead of double quotes, or comments (//), which standard JSON doesn't allow.

2. Regex Tester

Use it when you're writing a pattern for validation, search-and-replace or log parsing and want to see what it really matches.

The Regex Tester has three inputs: Pattern, Flags and Test text. Matches are highlighted live in the text as you type, and a table underneath lists each match with its position (index) and any capture groups. The first 200 matches are listed, with the total count shown above the table.

Tips:

  • The tool always adds the g flag so it can find every match. Add i for case-insensitive or m for multi-line anchors.
  • It uses JavaScript's regex engine, so behaviour matches what you'd get in a browser or Node.js. Syntax from other languages, such as possessive quantifiers, may not work.
  • If the pattern is invalid, the error message replaces the highlight area, which is handy for spotting an unclosed bracket.

3. JWT Decoder

Use it when you need to check what's inside a JSON Web Token: the user ID, roles, issuer or expiry time.

Paste a token into the JWT Decoder and you'll see the header and payload as formatted JSON. If the payload has an exp claim, the tool shows the expiry as a readable date and says whether the token is expired or still valid by your device's clock.

Two important points:

  • The signature is not verified. Decoding only shows what the token claims. Never treat a decoded token as trusted; verification has to happen on your server with the secret or public key.
  • Decoding happens locally, which makes it safer than pasting real tokens into a random website. Still, treat live tokens like passwords.

4. Base64 Encoder / Decoder

Use it when you're dealing with Basic Auth headers, data URLs, email attachments or API fields that carry Base64.

The Base64 tool has an Encode and a Decode mode for text, and it handles Unicode properly, so accented letters and emoji survive the round trip. Below that, you can drop in a file and get it back as a full data URL (for example data:image/png;base64,...), ready to paste into CSS or HTML.

Remember: Base64 is an encoding, not encryption. Anyone can decode it.

5. URL Encoder / Decoder

Use it when a query parameter contains spaces, &, ? or non-English characters, or when you're trying to read a long tracking link.

The URL Encoder encodes text the way a single URL component should be encoded (so & becomes %26 and a space becomes %20). In Decode mode, it also turns + signs into spaces, which is how form data is often sent.

Encode individual values, not a full address. Encoding https:// itself turns the colon and slashes into codes, which isn't what you want.

6. CSV to JSON (and JSON to CSV)

Use it when you need to turn a spreadsheet export into data for an API or a script, or flatten API output for Excel.

In the CSV to JSON Converter, choose the direction and the separator: comma, semicolon (common in European Excel exports) or tab. In CSV-to-JSON mode, the first row becomes the keys and number-looking values become real numbers. In JSON-to-CSV mode, the tool collects every key across all objects for the header row and wraps values in quotes when they contain separators, quotes or line breaks. You can copy the result or download it.

7. SQL Formatter

Use it when a query was generated by an ORM, copied from a log, or written on one long line.

Paste it into the SQL Formatter and it puts major clauses like SELECT, FROM, WHERE, JOIN, GROUP BY and ORDER BY on their own lines, indents AND / OR conditions, and breaks column lists after commas. Tick UPPERCASE keywords for the classic style, or untick it for lowercase.

It's a readability formatter, not a SQL parser, so it won't catch syntax errors. Also check queries that contain commas inside string values, since those get line breaks too.

8. UUID Generator

Use it when you need test IDs, seed data or unique keys.

The UUID Generator creates random version 4 UUIDs using your browser's built-in secure random generator. Set How many (up to 1,000 at a time) and tick UPPERCASE if your system expects capital letters. Copy the whole list in one click.

Problem Tool

Privacy

All eight tools run entirely in your browser. Nothing you paste, whether JSON with customer data, tokens or SQL with table names, is sent to DoraPDF's server.

FAQ

Are these developer tools free? Yes, all of them, with no sign-up.

Does the JWT decoder check if a token is genuine? No. It decodes the header and payload only. Signature verification must happen on your backend.

Is my data uploaded anywhere? No. Processing happens locally in your browser tab.

Can the JSON validator handle large files? It handles typical API responses and config files comfortably. Very large files depend on your device's memory, since everything runs in the browser.

Which UUID version does the generator create? Version 4 (random) UUIDs.
